newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Panel says EU research programme needs major overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Panel says EU research programme needs major overhaul.

text.p: The European Union's multibillion-dollar research programme is not fulfilling its promise and needs a major overhaul, an independent panel of business leaders, scientists and politicians said on Wednesday.

The 12-member panel said the EU's programme, which channels about 3.5 billion Ecus a year to research projects in areas ranging from biotechnology to transport, lacked focus and was in the grip of national and sectoral interests.
"This is not the fault of individuals but of a structure which inhibits the formulation of real strategy and makes effective implementation difficult," said the report.

The panel, headed by Etienne Davignon, chairman of Belgian holding company Societe Generale de Belgique and a former EU Commissioner, conducted a five-year assessment of the EU's multiannual research "framework programmes" at the request of EU governments.

It concluded that the programmes were unable to develop a pan-European strategy focus because they were hampered by cumbersome decision-making procedures -- especially by the requirement that all 15 EU countries adopt them unanimously.
"If each member state has the right of veto, it is pure hypocrisy to suggest that you want to have a strategic focus," Davignon told a news conference.

The panel urged the EU, which is in the process of drawing up the Fifth Framework Programme to begin in 1999, to focus on projects that add "European value" -- such as large-scale research facilities or the development of "industrial platforms", or technologies and standards, that can compete globally in areas such as telecommunications.

It said the inter-governmental conference now considering reforms to the EU treaty should ensure that the framework programmes can be adopted by qualified majority vote. The European Commission should also be given more power to manage the programmes, backed up by a new committee of high-level independent experts, it added.
That would give the projects, which are now locked into decisions for up to seven years, more flexibility to adapt to scientific and technological changes, the report said.
Research Commissioner Edith Cresson told reporters she agreed that the EU treaty should be amended to introduce more flexible decision-making procedures.
